title: Anycast
explain: Anycast announces the same IP address from many locations over BGP, so each client's packets simply follow the best route to whichever site the network considers closest. I use it to give users one address everywhere and to fail a site over fast: drain it by withdrawing its route instead of waiting for DNS caches.
model:
**Unicast:** one IP points to one server in one place. **Anycast:** the *same* prefix is announced from many sites; every router along the path picks the best BGP route it knows (broadly the shortest AS path, subject to policy).

```
announce 203.0.113.0/24 from  Frankfurt, Virginia, Singapore
client in Paris  --> best BGP route --> Frankfurt
client in Tokyo  --> best BGP route --> Singapore
Frankfurt fails  --> withdraw announcement --> Paris reconverges to the next best site
```

**Why:** one address worldwide (no geo-DNS logic), failover in seconds to minutes by route withdrawal, and attack traffic, including DDoS, spread over many sites. DNS roots, public resolvers and CDNs work this way.

**Caveats:** "closest" means best path by policy, not lowest latency. Routes can change mid-flow, so one TCP connection's packets may reach a different site that has no state and answers with a reset. Common big-company design: anycast to the nearest edge, which terminates the connection and proxies over a private backbone to a region; see [load balancing](#/sd/f/load-balancing).

details.q: What decides which anycast site a client reaches?
details.a: BGP route selection along the path: usually the shortest AS path subject to operator policy, not measured latency. It correlates with proximity but can send a client to a farther site.

details.q: How does anycast failover compare with geo-DNS using 300 s TTLs?
details.a: A failing site withdraws its BGP announcement and routing reconverges in seconds to minutes, independent of client caches. DNS failover is bounded by cached answers, and some resolvers ignore low TTLs.

details.q: A WebSocket on an anycast IP is occasionally reset right after a routing change. Why?
details.a: Routing shifted, so later packets reached another site with no state for that TCP connection, and it replied with RST. Anycast guarantees reaching a site, not the same site over time.

details.q: How do you make anycast safe for long-lived connections?
details.a: Terminate TCP at a nearby edge that rarely flips, add client reconnect logic, or use protocols with connection IDs such as QUIC. Short UDP exchanges (DNS) are naturally a good fit.

details.q: Does anycast guarantee the lowest latency?
details.a: No. BGP picks by path length and policy, so edge-level steering and measured latency still matter.

details.q: Why does anycast help against DDoS?
details.a: Attack traffic enters at many sites and each absorbs only the share closest to its sources, instead of all of it hitting one location. A heavily hit site can also be withdrawn so traffic shifts elsewhere.

prompts.q: Explain anycast in about 30 seconds and name its biggest caveat.
points: Same IP announced from many sites via BGP
Routers choose the best route, so clients reach a nearby site
Caveat: path policy is not latency, and routes can change mid-flow

prompts.q: Walk through how a request reaches a healthy site, and what happens when the site dies.
points: BGP propagates and each router picks its best route
Client packets follow it to one site; the edge terminates and forwards inward
Failure: withdraw the route, traffic reconverges on the next-best site

prompts.q: Compare anycast and geo-DNS for steering users, and say when you would pick each.
points: Anycast: network picks, fast failover, one IP, flow can flip sites
Geo-DNS: application picks, can use latency or capacity data, cache-bound failover
Anycast suits edges and UDP or short exchanges
Often combined: anycast to the edge, then internal steering
